Guided Inquiry

The circuit

A resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C sit in series across an alternating supply of rms voltage V and angular frequency ω. The inductor opposes the current with the reactance XL = ωL, which grows with frequency; the capacitor opposes it with XC = 1/(ωC), which shrinks with frequency.

L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF are fixed here. The triangle has R along its base, XL−XC standing on it, and the impedance Z as its hypotenuse.

Voltage across one element

The same current passes through all three elements in turn. Can the rms voltage across the capacitor alone exceed the rms voltage of the supply?

At the resonant frequency

At ω₀ = 1000 rad/s the two reactances are equal: XL = XC = 100 Ω, with R = 10 Ω and a 230 V supply. How large is the rms voltage across the inductor there?

What the supply pays for

A supply holding Vrms across a current Irms must push out Vrms·Irms volt-amperes — the apparent power S. The heat actually produced in the circuit is the average power P.

As ω is raised from 500 rad/s to ω₀, what happens to S and to P?

Power factor

The ratio P/S is the power factor, cos φ = R/Z, and only the resistor dissipates: P = Irms²·R exactly, while the inductor and the capacitor hand back every joule they take within the cycle.

That gap is why an industrial plant running at a poor power factor is billed for current it never turned into work.

The Physics

The Impedance Triangle — and the Power You Do Not Get · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A resistor, an inductor and a capacitor are wired in series across an alternating supply. The sim draws their combined opposition to the current as a right triangle, beside the voltage and current waves.

What you'll learn

  • How R and the two reactances combine into the impedance Z and the phase angle φ.
  • How to read the voltage across each element and the two kinds of power.
  • What each control and read-out in the sim does.
R, L and C share one loop, so the same current passes through each. L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF are fixed in the sim.

What's on screen

  • Teal base: the resistance R, along the bottom of the triangle.
  • Orange leg: the net reactance XL − XC. It points up when positive and down when negative.
  • Hypotenuse: the impedance Z. The amber arc at the corner is the phase angle φ.
  • Wave panel: the supply voltage v as a solid line and the current i as a dashed line, two cycles of ωt.
  • Read-outs in the side panel: Z, Irms, φ, cos φ and the regime. The voltage and power displays appear as the guided inquiry reaches them. Free exploration shows everything.

03

The impedance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle

One current I passes through R, L and C in turn. The resistor opposes it by R. The inductor opposes it by the reactance XL = ωL, which grows with ω. The capacitor opposes it by XC = 1/(ωC), which shrinks with ω. At ω = 500 rad/s, XL = 50 Ω and XC = 200 Ω.

Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²),   tan φ = (XL − XC) / R
R lies along the base, the net reactance stands on it, and Z is the hypotenuse. φ is the angle at the base corner.

The net reactance here is 50 − 200 = −150 Ω, so Z = √(10² + 150²) = 150.3 Ω and φ = tan⁻¹(−15) = −86.2°. A negative net reactance is drawn downward and the regime reads capacitive: the current leads the voltage. A positive one is inductive, and the current lags. The current is Irms = Vrms/Z = 230/150.3 = 1.53 A.

See itOpen at ω = 500 rad/s, R = 10 Ω and Vrms = 230 V. Watch for: Z = 150.3 Ω and φ = −86.2°, with the leg drawn downward.
See itRaise ω to 2000 rad/s, so XL = 200 Ω and XC = 50 Ω. Watch for: the same Z = 150.3 Ω, but φ = +86.2° and the leg flipped upward.
04

Each element's voltage is I times its own opposition

The same I flows through all three, so each element takes the voltage that its own opposition demands:

VR = I R,   VL = I XL,   VC = I XC,   V = I Z
All are rms values. V is the supply.

At the opening setting I = 1.53 A, so VR = 15.3 V, VL = 76.5 V and VC = 306.0 V. The capacitor alone takes more than the 230 V supply. That happens whenever XC is larger than Z.

It is allowed because the three voltages are not in step. VL leads the current by 90° and VC lags it by 90°, so they point opposite ways and partly cancel. The supply is their phasor sum, √(VR² + (VL − VC)²) = √(15.3² + 229.5²) = 230.0 V. Adding the three as plain numbers gives 397.8 V, which is not the supply.

See itStay at the opening setting and read the voltage box. Watch for: VC = 306.0 V, the plain sum 397.8 V, and the phasor sum equal to the 230.0 V supply.
See itRaise ω to 2000 rad/s. Watch for: VL and VC swapping to 306.0 V and 76.5 V, with the phasor sum still 230.0 V.
05

At ω₀ the reactances cancel and Z falls to R

Setting XL = XC gives ω²LC = 1, so the resonant frequency is:

ω0 = 1/√(LC),   Q = ω0L / R
For L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF: ω₀ = 1/√(0.1 × 10⁻⁵) = 1000 rad/s.

At ω₀, XL = XC = 100 Ω. The net reactance is zero, so Z = R = 10 Ω, φ = 0 and the current reaches its largest value, I = 230/10 = 23 A. The triangle collapses onto its base.

The two element voltages are then VL = VC = 23 × 100 = 2300 V, which is Q = 100/10 = 10 times the 230 V supply. They are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the loop. A smaller R makes it worse: with R = 2 Ω, Q = 50 and each of VL and VC is 11.5 kV from the same supply.

See itTune ω to 1000 rad/s, keeping R = 10 Ω. Watch for: Z = 10.0 Ω, I = 23.00 A, and VL and VC both at 2.30 kV.
See itStay at ω₀ and lower R to 2 Ω. Watch for: I = 115.00 A and VL = VC = 11.50 kV.
06

Apparent power is V·I, and average power is V·I·cos φ

The supply holds Vrms while pushing Irms, so it delivers S = Vrms Irms volt-amperes. The heat actually produced is the cycle average of v·i, which is lower when the two are out of step:

S = Vrms Irms,   P = Vrms Irms cos φ
S is in volt-ampere (VA) and P in watt (W). cos φ is the fraction of S that does work.

At the opening setting S = 230 × 1.53 = 352 VA. With cos φ = 0.0665 (the read-out rounds it to 0.067), P = 352 × 0.0665 = 23.4 W. The sim draws both bars on one scale whose full height is V²/R = 5290 W, the power the circuit would take at resonance. The gap between the bars is the reactive part.

See itOpen at ω = 500 rad/s and look at the power bars. Watch for: S near 352 VA, P near 23.4 W, and the gap labelled between them.
See itTune ω to 1000 rad/s. Watch for: both bars rising to full scale at 5.29 kVA and 5.29 kW, with no gap left.
07

Only the resistor dissipates, so P = I²R

In the triangle, cos φ = R/Z. Since V = I Z, the average power becomes:

P = Vrms Irms (R/Z) = Irms² R
The power factor is cos φ = R/Z = P/S.

An ideal inductor and capacitor store energy in a field and hand all of it back every cycle, so their average power is zero. At the opening setting, I² R = 1.53² × 10 = 23.4 W, the same P as before.

Raising R to 40 Ω at ω = 500 rad/s makes Z = 155.2 Ω and cos φ = 0.258. The current is a little smaller, 1.48 A, yet P rises to 1.48² × 40 = 87.8 W, because more of the circuit is resistor. A plant with a low power factor draws I = P/(V cos φ), more current than its work needs.

See itRaise R to 40 Ω at ω = 500 rad/s. Watch for: cos φ = 0.258, I = 1.48 A, and the P bar near 87.8 W.
08

Where it matters

  • Radio tuning. A tuner is a series or parallel LC circuit whose ω₀ is set to a station's frequency. At ω₀ the signal drives a large current, and a high Q makes the circuit pick out a narrow band.
  • Power factor. Motors and transformers are inductive, so a plant draws more current than its real power needs. Utilities charge for that, so plants add capacitors to cancel part of the net reactance and bring cos φ back toward 1.
  • Component ratings. At resonance L and C each carry Q times the supply voltage, so their insulation must be rated for that, not for the supply.
09

Summary

In one line. In a series LCR circuit, R and the two reactances set one impedance Z, and that Z decides the current, the phase and the power.

Key points

  • XL = ωL, XC = 1/(ωC), Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) and tan φ = (XL − XC)/R.
  • Element voltages add as phasors, so VL or VC can exceed the supply.
  • S = V I, P = V I cos φ = I² R, and cos φ = R/Z. At ω₀, Z = R and S = P.

Common mix-ups

  • "No element can have more voltage than the supply." The voltages are out of step, so VC or VL alone can be larger. Only the phasor sum equals the supply.
  • "Power is V·I." That is the apparent power S. The heat is V·I·cos φ, and cos φ can be very small.
  • "At resonance XL = XC means no current." The two cancel each other, not the current. Z = R, so the current is at its largest.

Things to try on your own

  • At ω₀ with R = 60 Ω, find Q and VL. Q = 1.67 and VL = 383 V.
  • At ω = 2500 rad/s with R = 10 Ω, find Z and φ. Z = 210.2 Ω and φ = +87.3°.
  • At ω = 700 rad/s, check P = I² R against V I cos φ. Both give 97.8 W.
